lesson: Paint the change; do not cut and shift the part. When a sprite part must open or close inside an existing outline (a mouth, an eye), keep the original pixels in place and paint the change within the outline — for a mouth, grow a dark wedge downward from the closed mouth line, hinged at the jaw corner, clip inner detail (tongue) inside the wedge, and clip everything to the foreground silhouette. A cut-and-shifted segment leaves a doubled outline and a smeared, speckled edge that survive later patch fixes. Basis: in the 2026-10-26 wolf face GIF, the translated chin produced exactly those two defects; they were found only by a full-resolution, frame-by-frame comparison against the original after Fujii's second correction, and the paint-only redesign removed the whole defect class because no seam can exist. Limit: this covers changes expressible as interior growth or darkening within an existing outline. Articulated limbs still need segmentation, with joint caps and the same full-resolution verification.

lesson: Never overwrite a delivered filename. A revision delivered under the same name may never reach the receiver: the client can keep showing a cached older version while the file on disk is already new, and the receiver will rightly report that the change 'is not there'. Allocate every delivered revision a fresh versioned name, <slug>_vNNN.<ext> with NNN = the largest existing version for that slug + 1, zero-padded; let the build script allocate it and assert the target does not exist. Basis: on 2026-10-26 the hinomaru-eye GIF was correct in the file (verified pixel by pixel) while Fujii's app still showed the older blue-eyed version; on 2026-10-27 Fujii marked this 'super important' and directed that it be prevented by a mechanism, elegantly using numbers, not by a promise (his words: 絶対に、こうならない仕組む、例えば、番号等を上手くエレガントに工夫して、活用して下さい！). Limit: versioned names guarantee that no existing delivered file is overwritten; they cannot force every client to refresh, so the new name itself is the delivery mechanism.

lesson: One mechanism per effect. If two mechanisms produce the same visible effect, they will overlap, read as a defect, and make tuning ambiguous; remove the redundant one instead of coordinating both. Basis: the wolf GIF had a long closed-eye stretch during the howl (driven by the swell curve) and, added later, a blink — two different ways of closing the eye. Fujii identified the overlap and directed that the closed-eye part be deleted; the eye is now always open and the blink (twice per cycle, ~0.24s each) is the only closing event, which also simplified the parameter sheet (the slow eye curve was abolished). This is an instance of the standing keyword エレガント in the programming sense: simple, non-redundant design. Limit: a distinct expressive state (sleeping, stunned) is a different effect, not an overlap; judge by effect, not by part.

lesson: Before claiming a fix, verify every frame at full resolution against the original — and separate 'the file is wrong' from 'the delivery did not arrive'. Twice in the 2026-10-26 GIF work the assistant claimed fixes that Fujii then corrected: the cheek stick-line (a patch that left the real doubled-outline and smudge defects untouched) and the eye colour (correct in the file, invisible on his screen due to caching). The checks that actually settled both were pixel-level: all-frames contact sheets, close crops of the changed area, and sampling the delivered file's own pixels. Limit: verification covers the file and the frames inspected; client-side display cannot be inspected directly, which is why the versioned-name lesson exists alongside.
